Last updated November 14, 2026.

South Dakota property tax is assessed and collected at the local level, and owners can appeal an assessment.

What the official sources say

  • Appeal to the local board of equalization is perfected by mailing or filing a notice of appeal with the clerk of the local board; a mailed appeal's postmark is conclusive on timeliness. (SDCL 10-11-16; source)
  • The clerk of the local board must be notified of the appeal no later than the Thursday preceding the third Monday in March. (SDCL 10-11-16; source)
  • An appeal from the local board to the county board of equalization must be mailed or filed with the county auditor on or before the first Tuesday in April. (SDCL 10-11-23; source)
  • The director of equalization must assess each tract of real property at its fair market value, using the cost, market and income approaches. (SDCL 10-6-119; source)
  • Former SDCL 10-6-33 (valuation basis) was transferred to SDCL 10-6-119. (SDCL 10-6-33; source)
  • South Dakota sells tax certificates; a tax deed proceeding may begin three years after the certificate sale and within six years. (SDCL 10-25-1; source)
  • Any person may redeem a tax certificate before a tax deed issues by paying the certificate sum, interest and subsequent taxes. (SDCL 10-24-1; source)

Who sets and collects property tax in South Dakota?

Three county offices do the work, and the state does none of the collecting. The county Director of Equalization values the property, the county Auditor turns the requests of each taxing district into levies, and the county Treasurer collects the bill.

The Department of Revenue's Property Tax 101 sheet says the state does not collect or spend any property tax revenue. Taxing districts include cities, counties, townships, school districts and special districts such as fire, ambulance, water and road.

If your question is about the value on your assessment notice, call the Director of Equalization. If it is about the bill, call the Treasurer. The department keeps contact lists for both on dor.sd.gov.

How is a South Dakota home valued and taxed?

A home is assessed at full and true value, which is its market value, as of November 1. The law then equalizes that value to 85 percent to get the taxable value, and the levy is applied to the taxable value.

Assessors combine three approaches for non-agricultural property: cost, market and income. The department says the market and cost approaches are the most common. Agricultural land is valued by a separate productivity formula.

The department's own example makes the math clear. A home with a full and true value of $120,000 has a taxable value of $102,000 after the 0.85 factor. A levy is expressed as dollars per thousand of taxable value, so at $10 per thousand a $150,000 value produces a $1,500 bill in the department's example.

DateWhat happens
November 1Legal assessment date
March 1Assessment notices mailed
March to JuneAppeal process
October 1Taxing district requests due to the County Auditor
NovemberAuditors calculate levies by November 1, and the Department of Revenue certifies them
January 1Tax bills mailed, and taxes due and payable

The department's example runs this way: a home assessed for the 2021 assessment year is valued as of November 1, 2020, and the taxes are payable in 2022. In other words, you pay on a value established the year before.

What is the owner-occupied classification and does it carry over to a buyer?

The owner-occupied classification lowers only the school general fund levy for a primary residence, and it ends when the house is sold. The department's July 2026 fact sheet says the status continues until the home is sold or its use changes, so the buyer has to apply again.

Other levies, such as county, city and school special education, are the same for every type of property. An owner can be a joint tenant, a life estate owner, a trust beneficiary or a contract for deed buyer, among others, and the dwelling must be the owner's principal residence.

  • Qualifying property: a house, condominium, townhome, manufactured home or a building of four or fewer family units.
  • One per person: an owner can claim the status on only one property statewide.
  • Deadline: the certificate goes to the Director of Equalization by March 15 of the current year.
  • Check your bill: an 'OO' or similar abbreviation on the assessment notice or tax bill shows the status.

The 2026 appeal guide lists the tests for appealing a denial: ownership and occupancy on November 1, 2025, that it is the only property you own with the status, that it is your principal residence, and that the certificate was filed by March 15, 2026.

When are South Dakota property taxes due, and what does late cost?

Bills are due January 1 and can be paid in two halves, by April 30 and by October 31. Under SDCL 10-21-23, the first half is delinquent May 1 and the second half November 1.

From the delinquency date, interest is added on the first of each month at the Category G rate set in SDCL 54-3-16. Taxes of fifty dollars or less must be paid in full by April 30. When the due date lands on a weekend, the tax is due on the last working day, and a payment postmarked by the last day before delinquency counts.

County offices add their own details, so read the treasurer's page for the county you are in.

  • Minnehaha County says taxes are delinquent May 1 and November 1 and a 10 percent annual penalty applies, described on the page as .83333 per month.
  • Brookings County does not accept partial payments for taxes that are due or delinquent, and in-person credit card payments carry a 2.5 percent fee.
  • Mead County's treasurer says delinquent taxpayers cannot pay online, returned payments carry a $40 fee, and a tax certificate sale is held in December.

What is the 2026 appeal calendar for a high assessment?

The first appeal goes to the local board of equalization, and the 2026 deadline to mail or file it was March 12. The Department of Revenue's 2026 appeal guide says you must appeal first to the local board or you lose your rights to the later boards.

Two groups skip that step: non-residents, who live outside the local board's jurisdiction, and owners in unorganized townships, who go straight to the county board. Some jurisdictions use a consolidated board, and your assessment notice tells you which applies.

Stage (2026 dates)Deadline or windowStatute cited
Assessment notices mailedMarch 1SDCL 10-6-154
Written appeal to the local board clerkMarch 12SDCL 10-11-16
Local board meetsMarch 16 to 20SDCL 10-11-13, 10-11-14
Written appeal to the county auditorApril 7SDCL 10-11-23
County board meetsApril 14 to May 5SDCL 10-11-25
Appeal to the Office of Hearing ExaminersMay 15SDCL 10-11-42
Circuit court, from the county board or OHEWithin 30 days of noticeAppeal guide

The calendar moves each year, so use the guide for the current year. A written appeal can be a letter, an email or a signed PT17 form, and it needs your name, the legal description and a short reason. You also need evidence, such as sales of similar properties. Saying the value is too high is not enough.

What relief programs exist for owners, and how do they affect a sale?

The Department of Revenue lists several programs, and a few of them end or come due when the property is sold. The homestead exemption is the one sellers should know about because it defers taxes instead of removing them.

  • Homestead exemption: delays payment of property taxes until the property is sold. The taxes are a lien, and they must be paid with interest before the property can be transferred. The 2026 programs list gives age 70 or older and an April 1 deadline.
  • Assessment freeze: for owners 65 or older or legally disabled who own and occupy the home, stopping the assessed value from rising. Income limits apply, and the deadline is April 1.
  • Disabled veteran exemption: the first $200,000 of valuation is exempt for a veteran rated permanently and totally disabled, with a November 1 deadline. It lasts until the property is transferred or sold.
  • Paraplegic veteran exemption: exempts the property from all property taxes until transfer or sale.

The 2026 list also describes three legislative changes. SB 216 (2025) caps annual growth in owner-occupied valuation at 3 percent per county and local budgets at 3 percent, temporarily for five years. SB 245 (2026) uses sales tax revenue to lower school levies. SB 96 (2026) lets counties add a local sales tax of up to 0.5 percent to credit owner-occupied property taxes. The department's own note says layout makes some of those details hard to match, so confirm with the Property Tax Division at 1-800-829-9188, option 2.

What happens if taxes go unpaid?

South Dakota sells tax certificates on delinquent real estate, and the certificate holder can later seek a tax deed. Under SDCL 10-25-1, a tax deed proceeding is started after three years from the certificate sale and within six years of it, if the certificate has not been redeemed.

Anyone may redeem a certificate before a deed issues. Under SDCL 10-24-1, the redeeming party pays the treasurer the sum on the certificate, interest at the rate the property sold for, other taxes paid since then and interest on those. The treasurer records the redemption and gives a receipt.

That sequence gives an owner time, but the cost grows. The statutes do not set a fixed redemption price, so ask the treasurer for the current payoff. Mead County's treasurer publishes delinquent real estate in public notices before its December sale.

How are taxes handled when you sell?

Taxes follow the property to the county where it sits, and the county Treasurer is the office that can tell you what is owed. A homestead deferral, if you have one, is a lien that must be paid with interest before the property can be transferred.

The seller also pays the state's transfer fee, fifty cents for each five hundred dollars of value under SDCL 43-4-21. The Department of Revenue lists a Certificate of Real Estate Value form, PT 56, on its forms page, so ask the title company whether your deed needs it.

A cash sale does not change these steps. It only removes the wait for a buyer's loan, which helps if a deadline such as April 30 or October 31 is close. We buy houses in South Dakota as they are, and an offer has no obligation attached.

More questions about South Dakota Property Tax Guide

Who do I call about a high property tax assessment in South Dakota?

Start with your county Director of Equalization, who can explain how the value was set. If you still disagree, the first formal step is a written appeal to the local board of equalization by mid-March.

When are South Dakota property taxes due?

Bills are due January 1 and payable in halves, by April 30 and October 31. A half becomes delinquent the next day, May 1 or November 1, and interest then accrues monthly.

Does the owner-occupied status transfer to the buyer?

No. It continues only until the home is sold or its use changes, so a new owner must apply, with the certificate due by March 15.

Can I defer property taxes until I sell?

The homestead exemption defers taxes until the property is sold, for owners 70 or older per the 2026 program list. The taxes become a lien with interest and must be paid before the property can be transferred.

How long before a tax certificate becomes a deed?

A tax deed proceeding is initiated after three years from the certificate sale and within six years, under SDCL 10-25-1. Anyone may redeem before a deed issues.

Is there a statewide cap on assessment increases?

SB 216 (2025) caps annual growth in owner-occupied valuation at 3 percent per county for five years, according to the Department of Revenue. Check the department for how it applies to your county.

South Dakota Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property

Selling a South Dakota House? Get a Cash Offer

Last updated November 14, 2026.

South Dakota probate runs through the courts named in the sources below.

What the official sources say

  • Personal property may be collected by affidavit 30 days after death if the entire estate, less liens, does not exceed $100,000, and no personal representative application is pending. (SDCL 29A-3-1201; source)
  • Successors may file an affidavit for real property 60 days after death if the decedent's real property interest in the state is $50,000 or less. (SDCL 29A-3-1203; source)
  • Real property affidavit must be filed with the register of deeds with a certified death certificate in each county where land is located. (SDCL 29A-3-1203; source)
  • Both affidavits require that the decedent owed no Department of Social Services medical assistance debt for nursing home or institutional care. (SDCL 29A-3-1201, 29A-3-1203; source)
  • A purchaser or lender in good faith for value takes title free of estate claims when buying from a successor under a real property affidavit. (SDCL 29A-3-1203; source)
Selling in South Dakota?
We buy South Dakota houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Does a South Dakota house always have to go through probate?

No. South Dakota lets successors collect small estates by affidavit, and the house can pass that way if the decedent's real property interest in the state is $50,000 or less. Larger estates, or any estate where someone needs authority to sell, go through a court-supervised appointment of a personal representative.

The state's probate code is Title 29A of the South Dakota Codified Laws. The Unified Judicial System lists probate as a civil case type that covers estates, wills, guardianships and conservatorships, and the clerk of the circuit court is where an application starts.

The affidavit routes are optional shortcuts with strict conditions. Missing one condition, such as a pending application for a personal representative, takes you out of the shortcut.

What are the two small estate affidavits?

One affidavit collects personal property, and the other transfers real property. Each has its own waiting period and dollar limit.

AffidavitWaiting period after deathLimitStatute
Personal property30 daysEntire estate, less liens and encumbrances, does not exceed $100,000SDCL 29A-3-1201
Real property60 daysDecedent's interest in all South Dakota real property does not exceed $50,000SDCL 29A-3-1203

Both affidavits require a statement that no application or petition for a personal representative is pending or has been granted anywhere. Both also require a statement that the decedent owed nothing to the Department of Social Services for medical assistance for nursing home or other institutional care.

For real estate classified as non-agricultural, SDCL 29A-3-1203 lets the value be taken from the assessment rolls for the year of death. For agricultural land, the value is fair market value on the date of death.

How does the real property affidavit work in practice?

Every person claiming as a successor signs the affidavit. It is filed with the register of deeds, along with a certified or authenticated death certificate, in every county where the decedent owned land.

The affidavit has to say who is entitled to the property and on what basis, which can be the homestead allowance, the family allowance, intestate succession or the decedent's will. If the claim is by will, the affiant must state that an investigation found no later will. Each successor's relationship to the decedent and the value of the entire estate go in the affidavit, and everyone signing swears that false statements can bring criminal penalties.

  • Liens and debts stay in place: the successor must apply the property to liens, funeral expenses, administration costs and creditor claims.
  • The successor has the same protection and liability as someone who received a deed of distribution from a personal representative.
  • A secured creditor or judgment creditor keeps its rights against the property.

The statute adds a buyer-protection sentence that matters for a sale. A purchaser or lender in good faith for value, without actual notice that the transfer was improper, takes title free of estate claims and has no duty to inquire whether the transfer was proper.

How do you open a South Dakota probate case?

An applicant asks the clerk for informal appointment as personal representative. Under SDCL 29A-3-307, if at least 120 hours have passed since the death, the clerk, after making the findings required by SDCL 29A-3-308, appoints the applicant, subject to qualification and acceptance.

Informal appointment fully establishes the status, powers and duties of the personal representative. It can be ended under SDCL 29A-3-608 through 29A-3-612, but it cannot be undone backward in time. A nonresident decedent's estate has a 30-day delay unless the domiciliary representative is the applicant or the will directs South Dakota law.

Do not wait indefinitely. SDCL 29A-3-108 says an informal or formal probate or appointment proceeding generally cannot start more than three years after the death. Limited exceptions exist, including a later proceeding when no proceedings concerning the estate occurred in the three-year period, but the personal representative in that case has narrow powers and only administration expenses can be claimed.

Can a personal representative sell the house?

Yes. SDCL 29A-3-715 lists what a personal representative may do, and it includes selling, mortgaging or leasing real property of the estate for cash, on credit or for part cash and part credit, subject to anything the will or a court order restricts.

The same section allows a personal representative to acquire or dispose of land in this or another state at public or private sale. It also allows insurance, repairs, employing attorneys and agents, and paying taxes and administration costs. A will that restricts those powers, or a formal-proceeding order, controls over the default list.

There is a notice rule on sales where the fair market value is not readily ascertainable. At least 14 days before closing, the personal representative must give written notice of the intended sale to persons who have filed a demand for notice under SDCL 29A-3-204. The notice states the property, the purchaser, the price, the payment terms and the security if any payment is deferred.

  • Heirs who want a say in a sale can file a demand for notice.
  • Ask the title company what proof of authority it needs before closing.

What happens to the estate's debts?

Creditors have a limited window to present claims. Under SDCL 29A-3-801, a personal representative may publish a notice to creditors once a week for three successive weeks in a legal newspaper in the county. Creditors then have four months after the first publication to present claims or risk being barred.

Known or reasonably ascertainable creditors get written notice by mail or other delivery. Their deadline is four months after the representative's appointment, or 60 days after the notice is sent, whichever is later. A representative need not send notice to a creditor who has already filed a claim, been paid in full, or was neither known nor reasonably ascertainable within four months of appointment.

SDCL 29A-3-803 gives an outer limit for claims arising before death: they are barred unless presented within the time in the published or written notice, or within three years after death. It does not stop proceedings to enforce a mortgage, pledge or other lien on estate property, so a mortgage on the house survives probate. Ask your title company how it will be paid off.

How is a South Dakota estate closed?

In an unsupervised estate, the personal representative can close it by filing a verified statement with the court no earlier than four months after the original appointment. That is SDCL 29A-3-1003.

The statement says the claims period has run or a diligent search for creditors was made, that all inheritance taxes and state estate taxes due have been determined and paid, that the estate has been administered and distributed, and that a copy of the statement and a full accounting went to heirs and devisees and to known creditors whose claims are neither paid nor barred. The accounting can be waived if the people entitled to it consent in writing.

If no proceedings involving the personal representative are pending one year after the closing statement is filed, the appointment ends.

What does selling an inherited South Dakota house cost in transfer fees?

The state transfer fee is fifty cents for each five hundred dollars of value, paid by the grantor under SDCL 43-4-21. That applies to a normal sale from a personal representative or from successors to a buyer.

SDCL 43-4-22 exempts several estate-related transfers, including transfers under a decree of distribution in a decedent's estate and transfers between a fiduciary and a beneficiary to accommodate the fiduciary relationship. A sale to a buyer for money is a different transaction, so expect the fee on a sale unless your title company says otherwise.

Taxes on the house still follow the normal county calendar. The state Department of Revenue explains that property taxes are due January 1 and payable in halves, by April 30 and October 31. Our statewide property tax page has the delinquency dates and the relief programs for older owners.

When does a cash sale make sense for an heir?

A cash sale can help when an heir lives out of state, when the house needs repairs, or when carrying costs are mounting while the estate is open. It does not shortcut the probate steps above. Someone with authority still has to sign the deed.

We buy South Dakota houses as they are, including inherited ones, and an offer comes with no obligation. Talk with a South Dakota attorney about whether you need a formal probate, since we cannot give legal advice on your family's estate.

More questions about South Dakota Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property

How long do I have to open probate in South Dakota?

Generally three years from the date of death under SDCL 29A-3-108. A few exceptions exist, but waiting limits what a personal representative can do.

Can I sell inherited property in South Dakota without probate?

Sometimes. If the decedent's South Dakota real property interest is $50,000 or less, successors may use the real property affidavit 60 days after death, and a good-faith purchaser takes title free of estate claims. Otherwise a personal representative usually signs the deed.

How long do creditors have to file claims against an estate?

If notice is published, four months after the first publication. Known creditors who get written notice have four months from appointment or 60 days from the notice, whichever is later. All claims are barred three years after death.

Does a mortgage disappear when the owner dies?

No. SDCL 29A-3-803 says the claims deadlines do not stop a proceeding to enforce a mortgage or other lien on estate property.

Who pays the South Dakota transfer fee on a sale?

The seller pays, at fifty cents per five hundred dollars of value under SDCL 43-4-21. Transfers under a decree of distribution in an estate are exempt.

How soon after death can an informal appointment happen?

The clerk may appoint the applicant once at least 120 hours have passed since death, after making the required findings, under SDCL 29A-3-307.
